#1263. What needs to happen for Manchester United to get relegated from the Premier League?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It couldn't happen, could it? The answer to that is probably not but the fact that, after Sunday's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, Manchester United being relegated to the Championship is a prospect that can be discussed as anything other than rival fan fiction ought to terrify the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

A quarter of the season is gone. The table may not be telling us the whole story but it can no longer be dismissed like it can in August or September. You'll struggle to find many teams who can sincerely argue they've been mistreated by the fixture list and United are certainly not one of them. They are where they are, 18th, a point behind Coventry City and safety, and there is not much to explain that away.

That is why Michael Carrick had to go. On Wednesday morning, the 45-year-old was still taking training at the club's Carrington base but he is expected to be relieved of his duties once the United hierarchy have met in Monaco. There, the club's chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are expected to tell minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that it is time to part ways with Carrick. Meanwhile, talks have already begun for USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino to take the helm, returning to the Premier League two and a half years after leaving Chelsea and mere months after signing a new deal with US Soccer. It would appear that unfinished business in England -- and the Old Trafford vacancy to which he has been linked for so long -- has tempted the Argentine away on the eve of the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals.

The path Pochettino is now on is one fraught with risk. And yet coaching for survival and nothing else would be the latest in a line of clumsy decisions from the Old Trafford hierarchy. Projection models such as Opta's would probably make the case that this team is dicing with danger but, with a 22% chance of relegation, will probably be fine. Bookmakers too are pretty skeptical that United's 2027-28 will encompass trips to Blackburn and Millwall with eight or so teams priced as more likely to go down than the Red Devils. That will be informed by an analytics profile that really does not suggest United are one of the three worst teams in the Premier League.

Through 10 games, a sample size where expected goals (xG) is more predictive than goals and scorelines when it comes to future results, United have an xG difference of -0.27. If there is an average team in the division, it's Carrick's. Naturally, that is not good enough for a team with their aspirations. Another 28 games putting up those underlying numbers and United will live to fight another day.

Suppose they don't. As anyone that saw Sunday's game can attest, events with a significantly less than 22% probability can happen all the time. A team's xG profile doesn't always capture everything. If it did, Villa would have notably fewer than their 13 points. Things could go worse for United. Let's have a look at how that might happen.

Carrick departs Old Trafford with his reputation among the fanbase still intact. He might also find that future employers look more forgivingly on his time at United. His tally of 47 points from 27 league games was bettered only by Manchester City and Arsenal, a goal difference of plus-10 putting United behind those two, Bournemouth and Brighton.

Equally, momentum had turned. With a full pre-season to establish his ideas (rather than hone Ruben Amorim's), Carrick seems to have crafted a team who are less effective in attack and more porous in defense. The 4-4-2/4-2-4 in which his team line up out of position has been easily manipulated by superior teams and structural issues are not offset by intensity off the ball. United rank 15th for pressures applied and 10th for passes per defensive action, both measures of pressing applied by a team. Meanwhile, the attack has both been creating fewer chances -- the comeback against Villa notwithstanding -- and being more wasteful with them. It is a bad cocktail.

The risk would have been that United reaffirmed the commitment they made to Carrick after the three-goal defeats to Como and Bournemouth, one which always seemed to be conditioned on the imminent international break. Could anyone parachuted in at a moment's notice have done much better than four points against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa? The November international break has always functioned as a critical point for English clubs. Fail to pull the trigger now when there is time to get your feet under the desk and familiarize yourself with players -- who, for once, will have a few days back at the training ground after their commitments around the globe -- before the festive fixture list bears its teeth. In that context, sacking a relatively inexperienced coach like Carrick probably lessens the relegation risk somewhat.

So, in principle, does hiring Pochettino. Here is a coach with over 400 games at the helm of English clubs, whose first job in the country with Southampton has afforded him some experience of the tight margins needed to avoid the drop zone. It was his work at Tottenham that so enamored Sir Alex Ferguson. Over five and a half years he forged Spurs into contenders for (but not winners of) the biggest prizes in the sport. Aggressive, attacking football with a young side imbued with English talent: everything except the silverware screams Manchester United in their pomp.

The price of that success was Pochettino's identity and Tottenham's intermingling. No bad thing when you are as successful as he was at first but it may have given the Argentine an expectation about his role in club football that he has brushed up against in subsequent jobs. At Chelsea he took umbrage at the hierarchy's insistence on affording him young signings rather than the veterans he wanted. The idea that set pieces should sit somewhat outside his jurisdiction and under "specialists" was not popular. At Tottenham, Pochettino had become accustomed to working cheek to jowl with executive chairman and part-owner Daniel Levy. Chelsea, like most Premier League clubs, have established numerous layers between the man in the dugout and the owners. He may not lose his rag in the manner of Antonio Conte but Pochettino is a deeply political operator. Any man who is not afraid to say what he sees could create a great deal of friction when he sees what has been going on at United these last few years.

When he left Stamford Bridge the sense was that Pochettino was yesterday's man in the rapidly evolving world of the Premier League, even though in retrospect it appears he left strong foundations for Enzo Maresca to build on. That view was clearly not one that senior figures at United entirely discounted. After all, at the time they were seriously considering sacking Erik ten Hag after finishing eighth in the Premier League. Pochettino was among the names they considered before doubling down on the soon-to-be-deposed Dutchman.

That was not the only time United could have got Pochettino. Indeed, when he left Paris Saint-Germain in the summer of 2022, he was interviewed before Ten Hag got the job. That was the most formal approach but there was also the restaurant summit with Ferguson at a Mayfair restaurant when Louis van Gaal was on the brink. And of course there was the chance to hire the 54-year-old in that window earlier this year when Carrick's interim spell was coming to an end and Pochettino had not yet recommitted to the USMNT.

Going for a coach they have consistently decided is not the best option for them will now cost them $10 million for his compensation plus the cost of his sizeable staff. The evidence of PSG, Chelsea and the USMNT is he can deliver to (realistic) expectations. In all likelihood things stabilize under Pochettino, the specter of relegation cast off. The scenario where he takes them down? It probably reflects yesterday's man taking a job at a club still enamored with an outdated vision of management. Pochettino is probably the most Ferguson-coded manager United have employed since the great man's anointed successor. His intense style of play will need willing participants and even if he finds them, it will also take time. That much was as apparent at the clubs where it clicked -- one win in his first seven league games with Southampton, three in nine at Spurs -- as it was elsewhere. Time is not a commodity a side in 18th place can really trade in.

Though Phil Neville was quite scathing in his assessment of Noussair Mazraoui, Ayden Heaven, Leny Yoro and Diogo Dalot on Sunday -- "that back four gets you relegated" -- in pure talent terms United should be absolutely fine. You can question how many players in the squad make up the core of the title-contending outfit they aspire to be but there has been plenty of decent business done buying decent players from decent Premier League teams. Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha, (in theory right now if not in practice) Youri Tielemans.

Getting another left back and another forward in January would solve a few issues created by more injury-addled players. Then again so would the players on the roster executing better. United rank fourth in the league for non-penalty xG but 11th for goals. Maybe that is because of their wayward finishing. Opta's shooting goals added metric, which assesses the likelihood of a goal being scored pre- and post-shot, ranks this team 17th in the league on -3.57. You wouldn't expect that to hold all season long, particularly when some of the worst offenders are Bruno Fernandes and Cunha. Of course, if it did, then yes, United would be in real trouble.

The same at the other end. Yoro met a free kick with a fine header at Old Trafford on Sunday, drawing a springy save from a goalkeeper who could not stop the ball being turned in on the rebound. The slight issue is the goalkeeper was Senne Lammens and that was the fourth error leading to a goal that United have made this season. Low-volume statistics like these can occasionally betray you but in this case it speaks to a truth clear for all to see; the United defense is too slap-dashy. Young and old, players at Old Trafford have learned that basic errors rarely lead to lasting consequences. If this clumsiness continues -- and it should not be treated as a given that it does -- then the crisis could deepen.

It's worth saying from the off that if you're rooting for chaos you'd want to see Manchester United's numbers trend down quite dramatically for there to be much in the analytics that says 18th or worse. The "best" relegated sides of recent years are probably Leicester City in 2022-23, sent down to the Championship on 34 points and -0.39 non-penalty xG difference (npxGD) per game, and West Ham three years later. They slipped through the trap door on 39 points and -0.26 npxGD, just a shade worse than Tottenham. Manchester United have sunk to levels below that in past seasons but not this.

Right now there is a long way to go to catch up with the worst teams in the league so far. Ipswich Town have accrued points and look to be a hard out but they are averaging -0.67 npxG difference per game. They are the worst of the newly promoted sides but both Hull City (-0.5) and Coventry City (-0.48) are delivering worrying analytics. The former have the advantage of those points they accrued early in the season and Hull deserve credit for how sparky and organized they are given the talent deficit Sergej Jakirovic is working with. Apply some of those principles with United's talent and competence is no longer the limit.

It isn't just the promoted sides that look bad. Sunderland have a case of difficult second-season syndrome. The best that can be said for Newcastle is that, like Hull, they've banked some fortuitous points. We can maybe ignore Aston Villa given how rarely their xG reflects the results Unai Emery gets.

Then there is Crystal Palace and, well, yikes. In the six seasons before this one only seven teams have had a worse npxGD per game than Palace's -0.86, which is a true marker of inadequacy. These levels Pierre Sage has plummeted the Conference League winners to aren't much better than Norwich City in 2021-22, Luton Town in 2023-24 or the carnival of ineptitude that was Leicester and Southampton two years ago. Palace are bad. So, so bad.

At least they are in results terms. The talent doesn't seem that bad even if the drip-drip of departures over the last year -- Oliver Glasner, Maxence Lacroix, Marc Guehi, Eberechi Eze -- has lowered their ceiling. With a Thomas Frank in charge you could see them move back on the right path quickly. Maybe the northeast triumvirate swing upwards too. Suddenly then there might be a space opening up for a team that is both bad and unlucky. That is, of course, assuming that there are three spots opened up for relegated teams this season.

Of course Manchester City might yet have a spot in next season's Championship with their name on it. City were found to have breached 114 of the Premier League's rules by an independent commission, a verdict they are in the midst of appealing.

Separate to the process of establishing whether the commission erred in its duties is the matter of sanctioning City. That will be decided by the same three-person panel though it is not yet clear when the hearing will take place nor what the Premier League will expect. Given the abrasive language used by the league about one of its member clubs, it is hard to see them settling for a proposal that does not end with City out of the top flight at the end of the season.

The Premier League wants this process wrapped up comprehensively but swiftly. Much of the football world expects City to get hit hard, hence why bookmakers have Enzo Maresca's side among the three most likely teams to be relegated. A sweeping points deduction at the Etihad Stadium would be greeted with delight around Old Trafford for many reasons. The fact that it might insulate United from their own mismanagement is certainly one of them.

There are, however, no guarantees that this process will reach its conclusion before the end of the season. City could endure, dragging out a process they have made plain they believe to be compromised at its most basic principles. Can they keep the wheels spinning for another seven-plus months? Or argue their way to the sort of punishment that does not send them off the edge of the Premier League map? It may be hard to do but it is the sort of unlikely event that, for the time being, might be required to send United to the Championship.

#1261. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

After that? Liverpool swarmed over Arsenal, particularly in the first-half with Florian Wirtz’s free-kick cannoning back off the crossbar and Mac Allister somehow heading over. He was six yards out and unmarked, it was a glorious chance.

That was the hosts’ last tangible opportunity to score. As well as Arsenal defended, it was not a good afternoon for Liverpool’s forwards, Bradley Barcola in particular, although it was interesting to see Arsenal double-up on Rio Ngumoha when he came on. Liverpool take the free-kick quickly and Kerkez releases Isak down the left to lash a left-foot shot over the angle of left post and crossbar.

Madueke is booked for legging up Barcola who threatened to race away on a counter after Van Dijk had blocked Bruno’s shot.

Arsenal hold their nerve and their lines when Wirtz, Nyoni and Gakpo try to thread passes in to feet in the penalty area, managing to make the blocks as Liverpool keep probing.

There’s a groan when Gakpo’s cross from the right hits Bruno. Then Isak was caught offside when turning the ball around the corner for Wirtz to have a shot.

Arsenal set up solidly in defensive lines to stop Liverpool raising the tempo on which they thrived in the first half.

Araujo wends his way around Calafiori after good work from Isak and crosses towards the penalty spot. Gabriel hooks the ball away with Wirtz and Isak on their heels around the 18-yard line.

Victor Muñoz has gone through a rigorous half-time warm up, which indicates he won’t be far away from getting minutes. The Spaniard’s pace and directness on the flank is exactly what Liverpool need in the second period. You would anticipate, too, there will come a point when Dominik Szoboszlai is introduced. Liverpool aren’t out of this, by any means, but they need a step up again.

Liverpool re-start “kicking into the Kop” in the words of Ian Wright. A ling chip down the right gives Gakpo something to chase but he can’t get round Calafiori who shepherds it out for a goal-kick.

Liverpool will be pleased with their response to going behind but very frustrated also at not, at least, being level. Arsenal started superbly and got their goal but Liverpool have swarmed all over them since. It has been a bit too frantic at times. There have been a series of penalty appeals, most of which were rightly ignored. But Arsenal got away with one when Jurrien Timber clearly pulled at Alexander Isak’s shirt, preventing him from heading a cross. It is the kind of incident that really makes you wonder what the VAR is doing.

Arsenal have been on the ropes since opening the scoring as wave after wave of Liverpool attacks swarm towards their box. But so far they retain their lead but will have to adjust their midfield and forward lines soon as it’s been boy stood on the burning deck stuff from Rice at times. Mac Allister, who has become a beast in the air recently, should have equalised but seemed to stoop into it and get under it rather than heading it down.

Barcola is booked for catching Timber in a sliding tackle and his visible contempt for the decision means there will be no reprieve.

With two minutes of stoppage time signalled Arsenal are on a rare attack but Tozolis again doesn’t release the ball when he should and slows it down.

Liverpool seem intent on trying to score a perfect goal. The irony is that it’s old fashioned pace and being direct that is starting to unsettle Arsenal. Bradley Barcola, therefore, needs to step up. He’s been on the edges so far and it’s crying out for him to have a persistent run at Jurrien Timber and ask him some big questions.

Mac Allister misses a sitter. He eluded his midfield marker and met Kerkez’s perfect cross between the penalty spot and six-yard line but steered it over. Now it’s Calafiori’s turn to upbraid the players ahead of him.

Rice is becoming very annoyed about a lack of support from his front players in providing a viable outlet when he wins the ball. He is waving his arms and chuntering away.

Wirtz takes the free-kick bending it with dip and whip over Raya but into the heart of the crossbar. Arsenal butcher their counter-attacking opportunity.

Timber is penalised for a decent-looking tackle on Isak just outside the box on the Liverpool left. That comes a moment after the referee gave Liverpool a corner despite Mac Allister’s cross not touching an Arsenal player. They are going spare and one can sympathise with them.

There’s no room at all in the Arsenal penalty area as first Mac Allister tries to fizz a pass through the massed ranks then Isak weaves an opening for a left-foot shot that he smacks into the hoardings, 3ft wide and rising.

Arsenal enjoy a moment of respite on a rapid counter down the right but Bruno takes too many touches when found by Odegaard in the middle, 18 yards out, allowing Mac Allister to tie him up.

Sky digs out a replay from the 21st minute which clearly shows Timber with a fistful of Isak’s shirt that stopped him reaching a cross. But he, unlike the bench, did not appeal for a penalty. “He is nice,” says Gary Neville disdainfully.

Kerkez cushions a pass on his thigh when he ghosts into the centre-forward position and then tamely lobs a volley wide from 18 yards. Liverpool are swarming the Arsenal penalty area.

Liverpool are laying siege at the moment, snapping into tackles, putting in crosses, taking one too many touches to surprise Arsenal. Now Gakpo goes down in the box when confronted by Tzolis who does make contact but not enough for Madley or the VAR after a look.

Liverpool corner from the right. Van Dijk wins the header and Isak, creeping round Konsa, is there to tap it in, but Raya is alert and pushes it behind before Isak can pounce.

Tzoli’s cross from the left is met at the back post by Timber who tries to knock it back across the six-yard box to Havertz but Timber gets in the way.

Mac Allister’s crossfield pearler picks out Kerkez but he hits the first defender with his cross and Arsenal counter at pace and Madueke faces Kerkez up but dawdles instead of trying to dribble past him. He waits for reinforcements and then cuts it back to Bruno who bends a pass through the six-yard box from the right of the D that Tzolis slides in but just cannot reach

The Arsenal goal has been a real tonic for Liverpool who are now hounding Arsenal’s players when in possession and gorging on mistakes, roared on by a raucous crowd. The volume is as high as I’ve heard for ages.

Two close shaves for Arsenal immediately after the goal, Rice needing to get back to stop Konsa’s mistake giving Wirtz a path to goal and then Barcola fades a cross/shot from the left of the D just beyond the right post.

Liverpool 0 Arsenal 1 (Havertz) Odegaard who, with Rice and Bruno, have dominated midfield, triggers the press when Liverpool play out from the back, disrupting a pass then running back to collect his interception. He strolls forward and plays it to Madueke who waits for Rice’s run on the overlap. The England midfielder delivers perfectly from the right and Havertz is Johnny on the spot at the back post to crash a shot past the scrambling Alisson.

"Absolutely brilliant from Arsenal." Kai Havertz gives Arsenal an early lead at Anfield! ⚡️ https://t.co/eeyhRcLlel

Van Dijk semi-deliberately collides with Havertz after clearing the ball very forcefully.

Arsenal have come with one intention in mind, seemingly, and that is to spoil the game. Already in the opening 14 minutes we have seen Gabriel go down as if he had been cracked on the chin by Tyson Fury and now Kai Havertz has reacted bizarrely to a straightforward coming together with Virgil van Dijk. They are better than that, as they have just shown with Havertz’s opening goal, and Liverpool will have to be cute if they are to find a way back into the contest.

Odegaard pushes up behind Tzolis and frees the winger for a run into the box. Araujo stalsk him stride for stride and uses his strength to lever him off the ball which rolls out for a goal-kick.

Arsenal are dominating possession but when they go back to Raya he makes a rare error with his feet and launches a 50-yard pass over Madueke’s head into touch.

Nyoni gets away without a card after another foul, this one on Havertz when Nyoni’s touch let him down and he booted the Arsenal forward. Mikel Arteta is rightly peeved that the referee has let him off again. Youth buys you leeway with Andy Madley.

Liverpool counter at pace down the middle but Raya is very sharply off his line to deal with the long pass. That’s the source of all the jargon about ‘verticality’ both managers inflicted on us in the build-up.

Arsenal corner after Tzolis was given space to run into down the left but hit Jacquet with his square pass when he made the 18-yard line. Arsenal take it short and seem to catch Tzolis by surprise and he is quickly closed down before he can give it precisely back to Rice.

Liverpool work the ball up the left to Kerkez who pings it infield to Isak. he opens his body to spay it into the stride of Gakpo who drags a right-foot shot wide of the left post.

Kerkez knocks the ball out for an Arsenal throw but immediately gets one back for his side when Van Dijk bullies Havertz who was trying to shield it.

Gabriel milks the life out of a tussle with Gakpo, going down clutching his face when slapped on the chest. A great defender but a ridiculous human being.

Arsenal kick off attacking the Kop but do not retain possession from Odegaard’s forward pass and there’s some counter-thrust until Timber takes possession on the right and drives forward to give it to Odegaard who is clumsily fouled by Nyoni who catches his ankle with his studs. Would have been a yellow for anyone else, I’d say, and the timing also made the referee reluctant.

This is a big day for Andoni Iraola and his emerging team and it feels like the stadium has its mojo back. It’s colourfully, lively and noisy and You’ll Never Walk Alone is being sung as loudly at any point since Liverpool were crowned champions in the spring of 2025. There is a feeling amongst home supporters that they fancy this today: that, in itself, shows progress because it wasn’t the case when Nottingham Forest and Fulham were the first Premier League visitors this season.

Any problems, he says, “let’s have a sensible chat” and he reminds them that they are responsible for their teams’ conduct as the strains of You’ll Never Walk Alone die down.

And now wreaths are laid in memory of the fallen followed by the Last Post.

Liverpool in Ron Yeatsian all red, Arsenal in that hideous faded yellow and blue. The yellow on Arsenal away kits should always be bright primrose. She didn’t wear a mustard ribbon did she, in the merry month of May?

Trey Nyoni is only the second ever teenager to make his first league start for Liverpool against the reigning English champions, after Raheem Sterling v Man City in August 2012. #LFC

The Arsenal players have long completed their warm-up and returned to the changing rooms. Liverpool have stayed out on the pitch and have just been involved in a lengthy team huddle with Virgil van Dijk conducting his own team talk in front of the Kop before they disperse and head back down the tunnel.

"He's brought a spirit that Liverpool really lacked last season" Jamie Carragher on the Liverpool fans taking to Ronald Araújo 🤝 https://t.co/dleLirsm2v

It’s not about me [being brave in picking Nyoni], it’s about Trey. In training he has shown he has the level. For us he’s very good without the ball. It’s a big challenge for him but [he is ready].

He is young but covers a lot of space. He is aggressive as well without the ball, calm in possession, good communicating with his team-mates which is good when you know how Arsenal play. You need a lot of change of marks [positions]. There have to be a lot of things done there in the middle and he has done that in other games.

The aggression we had [against Brighton, never resting] in their structures, we go again, recover, go vertical, attack the spaces in behind, win the chance battle, one v one situations. Don’t concede territory against teams like Brighton and Arsenal. We have to be as aggressive as we were in that match.

Teams like this don’t give you easy situations [to score]. We have to be good in one v one, shots from outside the box, finishes, set plays – we should be a team that is strong in set plays. You won’t get many chances against Arsenal and when you have one you’ve got to grab it.

Yes we had good results with Bournemouth against Arsenal but the strengths of my team in Liverpool are different so you have to approach it in a different way. There are things I can use [from Bournemouth] but not a lot.

Arsenal have lost three of their last four games against Bournemouth when Iraola was in charge.

We have been very close [to winning at Anfield in the last four seasons] but moments have decided those games. We have to be really precise in those moments for victory here and that has to be the case today.

Every manager has different solutions and a different approach and Andoni’s is very clear. We expect a different game to that one [last year when Arne Slot’s side won 1-0]. It is a team that is very vertical with a real capacity to create chaos from almost all situations. They’re very good in the high press with great individuals.

[On selection] We have had issues this week with ankles and other things and had to be smart how we manage the minutes today to have players for the minutes they are available for. The conditions and the context force you to make certain decisions [on Tzolis coming straight back in after a month out].

We can’t wait. This is the kind of opportunity, challenge, mission you want to come to Anfield for.

There will be a commemoration of the fallen and pledge to care for the living before the match.

Arsenal  Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Rice, Guimaraes, Odegaar; Madueke, Havertz, Tzolis. Substitutes Arrizabalaga, Mosquera, White, Hincapié, Eze, Gyokeres, Merino, Zubimendi, Lewis-Skelly.

Five changes: from the victory over Everton, Timber comes in for White, Calafiori for Lewis-Skelly, Bruno for Merino, Havertz for Gyokeres and Tzolis for Eze.

🟡 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🔵 Your Gunners, representing north London 👊 🤝 @deel

Here is a question I did not think I would be asking at any stage this season: will Liverpool win the Premier League?

It would be premature to describe this Sunday’s Anfield fixture as a title duel. Arsenal are better equipped to defend their crown, while Liverpool are a work in progress.

Whatever the outcome this weekend, Arsenal will leave Merseyside as the overwhelming favourites to claim back-to-back titles. They have a six-point lead over Liverpool. Should that extend to nine, Andoni Iraola’s primary objective coming into this season will remain unchanged; qualifying for the Champions League will represent a promising start to his reign.

What makes this weekend more significant is the champions will find a different Anfield to that which ended last season in such a downbeat mood, and came into this one uncertain of what was in store.

The discussion about what is achievable for Liverpool in the coming months is evolving by the week, the team bubbling along slightly under the radar.

There are several reasons why there are those who believe Iraola’s side might push Arsenal closer than anticipated.

Advertisement | GambleAware | 18+ Betting on the football tonight? Take a look at these tips and offers chosen by Telegraph Media Group.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool, who start the game in fifth with 15 points, and Arsenal, six points in front of them in second place. Anfield, that glorious night in May 1989 excepted, has not been the happiest of hunting grounds for Arsenal and though their record there recently – three draws in the last four visits – has perked up, they have gone 13 seasons without a victory, so long ago, in fact, that Mikel Arteta was in the side that celebrated Lukas Podolski  and Santo Cazorla earning them a 2-0 win.

Having already lost within the perimeter of the historic county of Lancashire this week, when knocked out of the Carabao Cup on penalties by League Two Fleetwood Town, the champions will be keen to end that barren streak and go into the 4.30pm kick-off on the back of three successive league victories following their defeat by Brighton. Points today, one or three, will put them ahead of Manchester City at the top of the table while victory for Liverpool would allow them to overtake Chelsea and move one point behind Brighton, the team they beat last week with the kind of performance that inspired talk of a credible title campaign.

For the visitors Max Dowman is suspended after his red card at Highbury and Bukayo Saka and William Saliba are sidelined for at least another three weeks with injury. In his pre-match press conference Arteta noted concerns about Noni Madueke (ankle), Declan Rice (thigh). Riccardo Calafiori (unspecified) and Christos Tzolis who has returned to training but all are expected to be available. Andoni Iraola has ruled out Jeremie Frimpong as well as long-term casualties Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley but hopes to be able to include Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Muñoz. Team news should come through at 3.15pm

#1260. USMNT coaching candidates: Could Pep Guardiola potentially replace Mauricio Pochettino?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With Mauricio Pochettino looking like he is on the way to Manchester United, there could be a major vacancy to fill for the U.S. men's national team with the head coach position. With a new national training center, an established team, and young players coming up from everywhere to push that squad, it's a job that should be an attractive one to managers around the world, depending on the direction that U.S. Soccer wants to go.

Pochettino was an appropriate splash hire ahead of the World Cup, and it's not surprising that a top team in the world still wanted him. But when looking to build a stable base for 2030, there's a chance that the powers that be would prefer a candidate who would be more bought into American soccer, so when looking at potential candidates to take the role, it makes sense to sound out both options, and here's the list it has come to:

The best American coach in Major League Soccer and someone who also got my vote for Coach of the Year after leading Nashville SC to a league-record 77 points in the regular season, B.J. Callaghan will need to be among the top contenders for the USMNT job if the U.S. Soccer Federation chooses to go with an American fit instead of another splash hire like Pochettino. He already has experience coaching and leading the USMNT during tournament play, leading the squad to the 2023 Concacaf Nations League title before heading to Nashville and turning them into one of the most complete sides in MLS. Callaghan has paid his dues, going from the college ranks all the way to the professional ones, and is someone with intimate knowledge of the American soccer system. If looking to go in a more traditional direction while also not shifting the vision of Olympic play, Callaghan is a solid choice.

While Nancy's time at Celtic after leaving the Columbus Crew was a moment to forget, not all of that was his fault, as the French manager has done nothing but succeed in his career, no matter where he has gone. Limit his resources, and he'll develop a system to get the best out of what he has; increase them, and he'll go toe to toe with everyone, and that flexibility is critical in international play. It's rare that you have your first-choice 11 available, and being able to work around that is what can make a difference on the margins. Nancy could want to still test himself in Europe but it doesn't hurt to call.

Currently overseeing the U-23s, the former Los Angeles FC manager would likely be in the USMNT succession plan for Pochettino. The goal was to bring both camps together as much as possible and ensure that they had a similar style, as plenty of players would go between both squads depending on needs. The issue is that this has all happened faster than anyone would've anticipated, since if Steve Cherundolo was going to take over the USMNT, that'd likely be a 2028 post-Olympic deal rather than right at this moment. But also looking at the performance of LAFC without Cherundolo, it's clear that he held things together plenty in that squad and that he could be a fit for the role; the question is just when.

You have to make the call, and it looks like they will. We all know what the answer likely is, but if there's an opening and the USMNT wants the best manager available, Pep Guardiola is right there. The former Manchester City, Bayern Munich and Barcelona boss is expected to be their top target, according to The Athletic.

They reportedly called Jurgen Klopp before hiring Pochettino, and this would be a similar scenario as Klopp is now with Germany. Guardiola isn't going to stay out of management forever, so why not try to bring him back in on the road to 2030? He would be facing similar issues to Pochettino of not knowing if he'll be a long-term fit for the role, but those aren't things that should come into play if the goal is to hire the best available manager who is a fit for the job.

A name that came up after the World Cup when decisions were being made on whether Pochettino should be extended, Roberto Martinez could come into consideration yet again. On paper, he offers a mix of European experience and the staying power of someone who has overseen multiple international sides for an entire cycle, but it's tough to say he'd be a good fit. Martinez wasn't able to lead Belgium's golden generation to a title and struggled to get Portugal to play to their talent as well. With a USMNT that have the world at their feet as young players begin to lead the way, it'd be better to go the domestic route before turning to Martinez.

#1259. Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cavity quantum electrodynamics1 with quantum emitters coupled to resonators provides a powerful platform for engineering light–matter interactions2,3 and exploring many-body phenomena4,5. In particular, superradiance6—arising from collective quantum interference among emitters—has been explored as a route to ultrastable continuous radiation7. However, engineering superradiance in the time domain to realize periodic pulsed sources or frequency combs remains largely unexplored. Here we investigate the non-equilibrium many-body dynamics of a driven spin ensemble coupled with an on-chip superconducting resonator and uncover a dynamical phase transition from continuous-wave to periodic pulsed superradiant emission. To quantitatively capture the observed dynamical phases, we introduce a driven-dissipative cavity-quantum electrodynamics model that elucidates how the periodic pulsed superradiant phase emerges from collective, periodically repeating spin dynamics stabilized by the interplay of coherence growth, disorder and dissipation. We also find that rare-earth ion spin systems with both optical and microwave transitions enable phase-synchronized, dual-rail superradiant frequency combs in both the microwave and the optical domains. Our results not only open new opportunities for atom-based frequency-comb sources and programmable superradiant generation, but establish a fundamental connection between periodic pulsed superradiance and the emergence of a continuous time crystal8,9,10 as a new non-equilibrium phase in driven open systems.

a, Detailed device schematic. A niobium film is patterned on a 500 μm thick 171Yb3+:YVO4 crystal. A 100 nm gold layer is evaporated on the back side, forming a weak optical Fabry-Pérot mode between the front and back chip reflections. b, Calibration of spin-cavity coupling strength. By optically pumping the population into the \(| \downarrow \rangle \) state, we probe the resonant spin-cavity coupling spectrum and its strength while avoiding superradiant effects. The blue data in the bottom subpanel correspond to the continuous-wave (CW) pump being off, while the black data are taken with a 400 μW continuous-wave pump. By fitting to a spin-cavity coupling model, we extract an ensemble coupling strength of \(\sqrt{N}g\approx 2\pi \times 1.1\) MHz, corresponding to a normalized coupling gnorm ≈ 0.6 < 1. The single-spin coupling, g = 2π × 10 Hz, and the effective ensemble size, N = 1010, are estimated from Comsol simulation and dopant concentration. c, Ensemble coupling strength, \(\sqrt{N}g\), as a function of pump power. We observe that the ensemble coupling strength increases with pump power, indicating a larger population in the microwave spin manifold.

a, A pulsed, transient optical pumping scheme that drives 171Yb3+ spins into the \(| \uparrow \rangle \) state. The resulting inverted spin polarization is resonantly coupled to a microwave cavity, leading to a superradiant burst in the microwave domain. b, Example of a delayed superradiant burst. A 1 mW pump is applied for 50 μs, after which a microwave superradiant burst is observed with a delay time τd. The superradiant signal is normalized by its peak-to-peak amplitude. c and d, Burst delay times, τd, and burst width, τw, measured as a function of the optical pump detuning, Δpump, which controls the optical transition strength from \(| g\rangle \) to \(| \uparrow \rangle \). A symmetric dependence of τd and τw is observed, with shorter delay times and narrower widths near resonance. This behaviour is consistent with the expected scaling τd, τw ∝ 1/N, as the pump detuning effectively controls the ensemble size, N, in the microwave spin manifold. Data points represent mean values, with error bars indicating the standard deviation over 300 repeated measurements.

a, Frequency-domain measurement of continuous-wave microwave superradiance, showing a much narrow linewidth of  ≈ 30 Hz. The inhomogeneously broadened ensemble line profile (dashed line) is overlaid for comparison. b, Dependence of the linewidth of continuous-wave superradiance on emission power, PMW. An inverse relationship between the linewidth and the emission power is observed, consistent with a noise-broadened Schawlow-Townes linewidth. The lower dashed line denotes the pump laser noise-limited bound. These results confirm that the disordered spin ensemble emits continuous-wave superradiance with a much narrower spectral linewidth. c, Continuous-wave superradiance emission frequency at different optical pump detunings. A linear correlation between the microwave emission frequency and optical pump detuning is observed, with a slope of  −1.23 kHz/MHz.

a, Four representative data traces under a 1 ms continuous optical pump. Random onset times of the emergent periodic pulsed phase are observed. b, Zoom-in of individual burst trains showing the distribution of burst onset times, {τk}, where k denotes the experimental repetition index. After an initial settling time, both the amplitudes, {Ak}, and the periodicity, T, become independent of k, indicating the establishment of a robust pulsed superradiance phase. c, Burst onset phases, defined as θk = 2π × τk/T (mod 2π), measured over 50 repetitions under identical experimental conditions. The phases are randomly distributed over 2π, demonstrating spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translation symmetry in the absence of any external timing reference.

a, Schematic of periodic pulsed superradiance, characterized by three parameters: the pulse-train periodicity T, the peak emission power Ppeak, and the average emission power \({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\). b-d, show fits to the experimental data presented in Fig. 3 of the main text, where T, Ppeak, and \({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\) exhibit good agreement with the expected scaling behaviours of T ∝ 1/N, Ppeak ∝ N2, and \({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\propto {N}^{2}\), respectively. Here, N is the effective number of spins in the microwave manifold, tuned via the optical pump detuning, Δpump. When sweeping Δpump, the optical pump power is fixed, corresponding to an excitation over an optical inhomogeneity Γop = 2π × 92 MHz in all three cases.

a, Relative contributions of superradiance (blue) and stimulated emission (red) to the emission strength in the periodic superradiance phase. b, Comparison of emission patterns between the many-body case with N = 1010 atoms (blue) and the single-atom case with N = 1 (red). For a fair comparison, the total effective cavity coupling strength is fixed to \({g}_{{\rm{tot}}}=\sqrt{N}g=2\pi \times 1\,{\rm{MHz}}\) for both cases. c, Comparison of emission patterns in the presence (blue) and absence (red) of spin frequency inhomogeneity, i.e., disorder. All simulations are performed using experimental parameters corresponding to the periodic superradiance phase in Regime III.

a and b, show simultaneously recorded microwave periodic superradiance and transferred optical periodic superradiance, respectively, over a duration of up to 100 ms. c, Zoom-in windows near 1, 50, and 100 ms showing synchronized dual-rail emission patterns, maintaining persistent and robust pulse periodicity without decay.

a, Microwave (blue) and optical (yellow) amplitudes, A(t), extracted from IQ detection as A(t) = ∣I(t) + iQ(t)∣. The I and Q signals, I(t) and Q(t), are measured continuously over 2 ms, capturing 30 consecutive superradiant bursts. The microwave and optical channels exhibit synchronized and reproducible temporal profiles. The grey shaded area indicates the noise floor determined from the optical signal, below which the phase extraction is not reliable. b, Normalized amplitude stability over 30 consecutive superradiant bursts. τ denotes the peak emission time, identified for each burst from the time-domain pulse train. The error bars denote the standard deviations of the microwave and optical normalized amplitudes, which are 0.009 and 0.05, respectively. c, Time-domain phase profiles, \(\phi (t)={\tan }^{-1}[Q(t)/I(t)]\), extracted from IQ detection. The microwave and optical pulse trains exhibit synchronized and reproducible phase profiles over time. Phase values in regions dominated by the optical-signal noise floor are greyed out, where large fluctuations are observed. The chirping behaviour during each pulse qualitatively follows the amplitude profile, which can be attributed to an effective Kerr nonlinearity induced intensity dependence. d, Phase stability over 30 consecutive superradiant bursts, zoomed in on the region above the noise floor. The error bars denote the standard deviations of the microwave and optical phase values, which are 0.03π and 0.11π, respectively. See Methods for details.

Cavity QED dynamics modelling and numerical simulation details, phase boundary estimation based on bifurcation and references.

#1258. With Manchester United set to hire Mauricio Pochettino, what other managers are available?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Manchester United have decided to make a managerial change during the November international break and sacked Michael Carrick after a challenging start to the season. The Red Devils have reportedly decided to hire Mauricio Pochettino, who led the United States men's national team at the 2026 World Cup and just signed a new deal with the American federation. However, Pochettino had a $10 million release clause in his contract and spoke multiple times about his desire to go back to the English Premier League, after coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea before making his move to the U.S.

Manchester United have also explored multiple options in the past weeks, and several names emerged as potential candidates for the job. Let's take a look at the top free-agent coaches currently available on the market and identify those who remain open to a move in the near future. For this specific reason we have decided to not include former Manchester City coach Pep Guardiola, who is not looking for a job in the short term.

The Spanish coach left Manchester City ahead of the summer of 2026 and decided to take a break from the world of soccer, despite having a concrete offer in the summer to become the new manager of the Italian national team. Guardiola sat down with the Italian federation but then opted to stick to his commitment to take a break. Furthermore, given his close ties to the Manchester City hierarchy and ownership, his name was never going to be considered by the Manchester United board. Here's a list of the top coaches without a job right now:

The former England national team manager is still searching for his next club after deciding to step down from his international role in order to return to club management. However, he appears unlikely to find a new position in the short term. This is a challenge currently facing several national team coaches, including former France manager Didier Deschamps. Manchester United had previously shown interest in him, but did not make a concrete approach in recent weeks, despite having the opportunity to do so.

The former Tottenham manager was one of the names that emerged in the past weeks for the Man United job. However, the former Brentford and Spurs manager is now in talks to become the new Crystal Palace manager after a disappointing start to the Premier League season, as the Eagles are currently at the bottom of the standings, two points behind Manchester United.

The former Newcastle head coach was one of the names on the list of the Manchester United board of directors in recent weeks. The English head coach left Newcastle in the summer and he's still under contract with the club right now. Any club looking to appoint him would first have to pay a release clause to Newcastle. Despite his Premier League experience, Manchester United did not consider him as a potential replacement. He is now likely to wait until the summer before deciding on his next career move.

An attractive name: the former German national team coach left his job in the summer after the disappointment of the 2026 World Cup, when Germany were kicked out by Paraguay in the round of 32 of the tournament. Nagelsmann, after coaching RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich before moving to the national team, is now likely to move to another league, and the Premier League is definitely a league that can potentially attract him. Let's now see if there will be a job available in the summer, even if the big clubs seem pretty stable at this stage.

The Italian coach is waiting for the right opportunity to come after the two years spent at Napoli, where he was able to win the Scudetto in his first season in charge, replicating the success he had at Juventus and Inter in his home country. According to reports, Conte would be keen for another Premier League experience after coaching Chelsea and Tottenham but he's not ruling out other clubs. However, Manchester United never made contact with his camp as they didn't want to hire the Italian manager to replace Carrick. Conte has often been regarded as a short-term appointment, having never spent more than three years at any single club throughout his managerial career.

#1257. OLIVER HOLT: Why England CAN now end 62 years of hurt - Thomas Tuchel is intoxicating and I'd tip Jude Bellingham to beat Kylian Mbappe to the next Ballon d'Or... plus my top 10 Three Lions performances

Published: 12:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:04 EST, 16 November 2026

The glum face of Lamine Yamal, head in hands, stared out from the front page of the Spanish sports paper AS as it sat on newspaper stands in Madrid on Monday morning. ‘Fin a la racha,’ the headline said. The end of the run.

For Spain football fans, England’s 3-2 dramatic victory over the world champions in the Spanish capital on Sunday evening made this akin to a day of mourning, the first time their team had tasted defeat in 44 matches, an end to a gilded period of invincibility.

For England, the feeling was very different. Because Sunday night in the cauldron of the Metropolitano felt very much like a beginning. Thomas Tuchel has been the head coach for almost two years but this was the moment of his true arrival.

This was the victory that freed us from looking back to the Groundhog Day pain of that World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in Atlanta last summer and allowed us to look forward to a future that seems luminous and full of hope.

This was the victory that allowed us to stop blaming Tuchel for what happened four months ago and start looking forwards again, dreaming about the glories that he might yet deliver. This was the victory that validated Tuchel and why the FA hired him in the first place. This was the victory that allowed us to believe he might be the Messiah after all.

This felt like the moment when he embraced us, with all our quirks and football idiosyncrasies, and we embraced him. He had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it with bells on. Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game and welded it to his principles and the result is intoxicating.

Thomas Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game to down world champions Spain

Once you have seen England play the way they did for an hour against Spain, you are lost. You are lost to the belief that the 62 years of hurt might really be coming to an end at Wembley in the final of the European Championship in the summer of 2028. You are lost to the idea that, finally, everything is falling into place.

For the 63 minutes up until the sending off of Elliot Anderson, I have never seen an England performance as good as the one that unfolded in the Metropolitano. Spain are the best team in the world and England outclassed them and stupefied them. They were better than them with the ball and better than them without the ball. They were magnificent.

Because of the context, because of the wonder of the stage, because of the odds they faced, England’s victory over Mexico in the grandeur and the mayhem of the mighty Azteca Stadium during the World Cup might edge Sunday’s performance but for pure football, what England delivered in Madrid demands comparison with the best they have played for many a year.

This year’s World Cup came just too soon but now Tuchel and England understand each other perfectly. And now England are purring. They have a manager who commands the players’ respect and they have a group of players that commands the respect of the manager.

Yes, it was just a Nations League group game but it was against one of the best national sides the world has ever seen. England worked so ferociously and attacked so fluently and defended so devotedly that they reached a level that drew admiration even from their opponents.

Many, many things will live long in the memory. James Trafford’s miraculous double save in the dying minutes gets better every time I watch it. Ben White’s goal channels the beauty of Carlos Alberto’s strike for Brazil against Italy in the 1970 World Cup Final, too. Let’s hope that strike, and his superb defensive performance, bring an end to the boos that have been his companion of late.

Jude Bellingham was relentless, tireless and glided through the game against Spain

Tuchel had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it

And then there was Jude Bellingham. Just when you think you can’t admire him any more than you do, he delivers a performance like the one he produced against Spain, a performance that lifted him above even the exalted company of the other players on two fine teams.

Bellingham was tireless. He was relentless. He glided past challenges. He thundered into tackles. He dominated midfield. He has the heart and the sheer brilliant indomitability that Bryan Robson possessed.

Bellingham has it in him to be England’s greatest ever player. He needs trophies to fulfil that destiny but maybe, finally, trophies are in reach again.

He has the team around him to do it, which Robson never quite had. Jordan Pickford is a good goalkeeper but Trafford might just be better. Ezri Konsa had his best game for England in Spain. White and Lewis Hall were superb at full back. Little more needs to be said about England’s front six. They are as good as any unit in world football.

Harry Kane, of course, was the best player in the world last year. Some seem to assume that the Ballon d’Or will inevitably pass to Yamal or Kylian Mbappe next. I think it is more likely to be Bellingham.

The man is a colossus. He is a footballer who has everything. He does not know how to be beaten.

Bellingham saw off Barcelona rival Lamine Yamal - and could beat him to the Ballon d'Or

With them together, the sky is the limit. And Bellingham has also proved to be a player of immense mental strength. It was not so long ago that people worried about his discipline but the fortitude he showed when he was being targeted by Argentina at the World Cup was the best answer to that.

He and Kane are England’s axis of ambition on the pitch. Tuchel is lucky to have them and they are lucky to have him, too. The coach has reached the point where his tactics and his team-building are bearing fruit.

Now England have a team-manager package that genuinely need fear nobody. The victory against Spain was a rehearsal for the bigger stage of major tournaments. Going down to 10 men after 63 minutes against the best team in the world might not have been in the script but that is what rehearsals are for.

After Sunday night in the Metropolitano, England are ready for their close-up.

#1256. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

Thierno Barry puts Everton ahead after Tyrique George's shot isn't dealt with by Lukáš Horníček! 🔵 https://t.co/oRXsrwbOhz

Everton had the lead and it was so easy and straightforward. They waited for Newcastle to give the ball away and then broke at speed. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was superb and forced a fingertip save from Hornicek. From the resulting corner, Hornicek was needed again to keep out Jake O’Brien’s header.

Newcastle tried to gain some momentum and finally created a chance. Harvey Barnes curled a cross to the far post. It bounced awkwardly but Anthony Elanga somehow failed to bundle it across the line.

It is always worth remembering that you only get a true reading of the Premier League table after ten games so this is a pivotal moment for both Newcastle and Everton as they play their ninth match of the campaign.

For Newcastle, a win tonight would take them up to seventh, just two points behind Chelsea in fourth. Despite the heavy away defeats and unconvincing performances, that would be an impressive start for a new manager. Matthias Jaissle has already felt the full force of the contrasting emotions on Tyneside in his three months in charge but big questions hang over his team. In particular, the “vertical football” style he brought from the Red Bull coaching school in Germany.

A defeat tonight, coming so soon after the 3-1 defeat in the Carabao Cup to Everton, will intensify the criticism of his approach.  It would also suggest Newcastle, despite all their positive talk over the summer, are nothing more than a mid-table team who will be looking over their shoulders rather than upwards this season.

A win for Everton will have the same uplift for David Moyes at Everton, also taking them up to seventh in the table. Given all the problems attached to their summer recruitment - or rather the lack of it - Everton will have defied the grim pre-season predictions heading into the second international break. The table is starting to take shape and so are the narratives around every club.

Newcastle and Everton meet for the second time in matter of days as the Premier League weekend concludes in the north east at St James’ Park. These teams encountered each other on Thursday night in the League Cup, where Everton won 3-1 at the Hill Dickinson to progress to the quarter-finals in that competition.

Newcastle, who won 2-0 at Crystal Palace in their last league outing, come into this game in 12th, with the chance to rise to seventh with a victory tonight. Their boss Matthias Jaissle has called on his players to use the defeat against Everton on Thursday as fuel for tonight.

“Now it is about taking that frustration into motivation for Monday and having that approach for the rematch,” Jaissle said. “We take it as a long-term journey, and our approach is to make progress, to see improvements. Now it is time to learn fast out of the mistakes that we just did. [There are] other phases where we can already see that we improved and this is something we can count on, we can build on, the good part. But football is also in the end about results so you need to avoid these simple mistakes.”

Everton, who have not won in the league since a 1-0 victory over Ipswich back in September, begin the night in 14th but, like Newcastle, could rise to seventh with a win. There are just two points that separate Bournemouth in seventh and Everton in 14th. Despite getting the better of Newcastle the other night, Everton manager David Moyes has warned that game will count for nothing tonight.

“It is a different ball game,” Moyes said. “Go to St James’ Park, on a Monday evening, they will get a crowd up there, you always know you are up against it. But we will go with confidence. We have played Newcastle a couple of times this year and done well, so we have to try and continue it. But Newcastle have got some really, really good players and players you have to concern yourself about.”

Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s squad for that League Cup victory because of an unauthorised absence from training and the 31-year-old is not expected to be involved tonight.

These sides were involved in a dramatic fixture on this ground last season. Everton claimed a 3-2 victory, with Thierno Barry earning them all three points in the 83rd minute, moments after Jacob Murphy had equalised for Newcastle. Team news from St James’ Park to follow shortly.

#1253. Premier League x Stonewall partnership ends, new LGBTQ+ campaign to be launched

The Premier League is set to introduce a new LGBTQ+ inclusion campaign after ending its partnership with Stonewall, the charity behind the widely recognised Rainbow Laces initiative.

Stonewallâs Rainbow Laces campaign, launched in 2013, became a fixture across English football, with players from all Premier League clubs wearing rainbow-coloured laces and captains donning rainbow armbands to promote acceptance and equality. The campaign aimed to support LGBTQ+ rights and foster inclusivity among fans and young people.

After over a decade of collaboration, the league will now lead its own campaign, timed to coincide with LGBTQ+ History Month in February, The Telegraph report.

"Rainbow Laces has benefited from a wide range of partners with a natural ebb and flow reflecting cultural and sporting changes," a Stonewall spokesperson told BBC Sport.

"Alongside other sporting bodies the FA has been instrumental in advancing LGBTQ+ inclusion at the grassroots level and more recently the Women's Super League has taken up the mantle as the women's game has grown - enabling Rainbow Laces to reach more diverse audiences."

Despite Stonewall's efforts, recent reports from Kick It Out reveal an alarming increase in discriminatory incidents in football, including rises in sexism, transphobia and faith-based abuse, with racism continuing to be the most prevalent issue.

Controversies around playersâ attitudes to rainbow armbands have also made headlines. Last season, Ipswich captain Sam Morsy declined to wear one due to religious beliefs, while Crystal Palaceâs Marc GuÃ©hi faced criticism for personalising his armband with the phrase âI Love Jesus.â

Additionally, Manchester United scrapped plans for LGBTQ+ support jackets after a player refused to participate.

With no openly gay or bisexual players currently in the Premier League, and the surge in discriminatory incidents, some question the timing of the split from Stonewall â an organisation highly respected for its work in LGBTQ+ advocacy.

Details of the Premier Leagueâs new campaign are still under wraps, but as the league presses âreset,â thereâs hope it will introduce a meaningful and effective initiative that advances equality rather than undermines it.
